o: Letting an app access a user's resources without their password
Encrypting database connections between services
Proving the owner of a website's identity
Storing user passwords safely in the browser
questions.w: OAuth 2.0 is a delegated authorization framework. Login (who is this user?) is added by OpenID Connect on top.

questions.q: Which grant type should a server-side web app or SPA use for user login in a modern setup?
o: Authorization Code with PKCE
Implicit grant
Resource Owner Password Credentials
Client Credentials
questions.w: The implicit and password grants are discouraged in OAuth 2.1. Authorization Code with PKCE keeps tokens out of the URL and protects the code from interception.

questions.q: Which grant fits a backend service calling another service with no user involved?
o: Client Credentials
Authorization Code
Implicit
Refresh Token
questions.w: The service authenticates itself with its own credentials and gets an access token for machine-to-machine calls.

o: It binds the code to the requesting client, so a stolen code fails
It encrypts the access token while it sits in the browser
It refreshes tokens without making any network call
It hides the client id from the person using the app
questions.w: The client sends a hashed code challenge up front and the verifier when exchanging the code. An attacker who intercepts the code does not have the verifier.

questions.q: Who are the four roles in OAuth 2.0?
o: Resource owner, client, authorization server and resource server
User, browser, database and firewall in the request path
Issuer, subject, audience and verifier of a token claim
Producer, consumer, broker and registry of a message bus
questions.w: The owner is the user. The client is the app. The authorization server issues tokens. The resource server hosts the API that accepts them.

questions.q: What is the `state` parameter in the authorization request used for?
o: It guards against CSRF by matching the response to the request
It stores the user's session on the server
It tells the server which scopes to remove
It chooses the lifetime of the token
questions.w: The client generates an unpredictable value, sends it, and checks that the same value comes back in the redirect.

o: The specific permissions the client asks for, such as read-only access
The lifetime of the token, measured in minutes or hours
The list of servers that a token is allowed to reach
The encryption algorithm that is used to protect the token
questions.w: Scopes limit what a token can do. Grant the least access needed, and let the resource server check them.

questions.q: Why must the redirect URI be registered and compared exactly by the authorization server?
o: An attacker could get the code or token sent to their own site
It makes the redirect itself a little quicker
It lets the user pick any site to return to
Browsers need it before they will store cookies
questions.w: Open or loosely matched redirect URIs are a classic way to steal authorization codes.
